target.title: fix(browser): stop screenshot vision-failure fallback from injecting raw base64
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running browser screenshot with a configured image-understanding model would have the session become unusable when that vision model failed: later `exec` / `read` / `browser snapshot` tool results were framed as image analysis until `/new`.

The vision-failure path previously fell back to injecting a raw base64 image block into the tool result. That image-bearing result is retained across recent completed turns, so it keeps re-entering model context and contaminates subsequent tool use.

This is the failure path described in #106703 (and the same root cause reported in #105305).

## Why This Change Was Made

The vision success path already returns a text-only description. This change makes the configured-vision failure path consistent with it: on describe failure, return a text-only result that reports the failure reason and keeps the staged outbound-copy path so the screenshot can still be shared explicitly via the message tool. Never write base64 image data into session/tool-result state on that path.

Scoped intentionally:

- Configured vision model throws: text-only (fixed path). A user who configured image understanding opted into text descriptions, so a transient provider error should not silently switch to dumping raw base64.
- Image understanding skipped / not configured (`describeBrowserScreenshot` returns `null`): still returns the raw image, so vision-capable primary models that rely on seeing the screenshot are unaffected.

## User Impact

When a configured image-understanding model fails during browser screenshot, the session stays usable: tool results remain text-framed, and the screenshot can still be shared via the message tool. Users without image understanding configured keep the previous model-visible screenshot behavior.

## Evidence

### Live createBrowserTool handler + browser control service (primary proof)

This is the proof ClawSweeper asked for: the changed `createBrowserTool().execute()` screenshot **catch** runs against a real managed Chrome tab through the in-process browser control service (not vitest mocks), configured vision fails through the real `describeImageFile` runtime, and a later `browser snapshot` in the same session stays text-only with zero image content blocks.

Reproduce (from this branch; needs local Chrome):

```
cd ~/oss-openclaw-106703   # or your checkout of fix/browser-screenshot-base64-fallback
git checkout fix/browser-screenshot-base64-fallback
pnpm install
pnpm exec tsx scripts/repro/browser-vision-failure-live-handler.ts
```

Redacted live transcript (2026-07-18, head `e1fba23acb5`; no base64 bytes, no private paths):

```
=== Step 1: start browser (real browser control service) ===

=== Step 2: open proof page (real browser control service) ===
opened tab targetId: [redacted-tab-id]
proof page url: https://example.com/

=== Step 3: screenshot via real createBrowserTool().execute() (configured vision fails) ===
[media-understanding] image: failed (0/1) reason=Unknown model
--- real screenshot handler catch path ---
content-block types: [text]
image content blocks: 0
text: [browser screenshot vision failed: Unknown model: openai/gpt-4o-mini]
[Screenshot saved to "[redacted-path]/outbound/[redacted].png". Use this path with the message tool to share the screenshot explicitly.]
details.vision.failed: true
details.vision.error: Unknown model: openai/gpt-4o-mini

=== Step 4: later snapshot in same session (real handler) ===
--- real snapshot handler (later tool call) ---
content-block types: [text]
image content blocks: 0
text: (wrapped external browser snapshot text; truncated)

result: PASS
```

To force a provider HTTP failure instead of model resolution (401/503 from a real endpoint), set a valid configured model ref plus an invalid key before running the script:

```
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-invalid-proof-key-replace-me
# ensure models.providers.openai.models includes your image model in the runtime config the script loads
pnpm exec tsx scripts/repro/browser-vision-failure-live-handler.ts
```

### Real-handler behavioral proof (vitest; mocked vision throw only)

The reported symptom is a session-state effect: on a configured image-understanding failure the screenshot tool result previously carried a raw base64 image block, which is retained across recent completed turns (`pruneProcessedHistoryImages` keeps image blocks from the last `PRESERVE_RECENT_COMPLETED_TURNS = 3` completed turns) and forces later `exec` / `read` / `browser snapshot` results into image-analysis framing until `/new`.

The proof drives the real `createBrowserTool().execute()` screenshot handler with the configured image-understanding call (`describeImageFile`) forced to fail, then drives a later `browser snapshot` through the same real handler. Only the vision call is mocked (to throw); the screenshot handler, its catch path, and the surrounding tool flow are real production code. It lives in `extensions/browser/src/browser-tool.test.ts` under the describe block `browser screenshot vision-failure session-contamination proof (#106703, #105305)`.

Reproduce:

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-browser.config.ts extensions/browser/src/browser-tool.test.ts -t "browser screenshot vision-failure session-contamination proof" --disableConsoleIntercept
```

Redacted transcript (content-block types and image-block counts only; no base64 bytes are printed):

```
--- real screenshot handler (configured vision failure) ---
content-block types: [text]
image content blocks: 0
text: [browser screenshot vision failed: vision provider unavailable (HTTP 503)] \n [Screenshot saved to "/tmp/openclaw-media/outbound/share.png". Use this path with the message tool to share the screenshot explicitly.]
--- real snapshot handler (later tool call) ---
content-block types: [text]
image content blocks: 0
text: <<<EXTERNAL_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT source="browser">>> \n ok \n <<<END_EXTERNAL_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT>>>
=== session transcript (redacted) ===
user: screenshot the dashboard and summarize it
toolResult(browser:screenshot): blocks=[text] images=0
assistant: the configured vision model was unavailable
user: now read the deploy status file
toolResult(read): blocks=[text] images=0
assistant: deploy is green
user: take a page snapshot
toolResult(browser:snapshot): blocks=[text] images=0
assistant: captured snapshot
total image content blocks across session: 0
--- no-vision path (unchanged) screenshot result ---
content-block types: [text, image]
image content blocks: 1
text: browser:screenshot
```

Reading the transcript:

- Real screenshot handler with configured vision forced to fail: the emitted tool result is text-only (`image content blocks: 0`), carries the neutralized failure reason and the staged outbound-copy share hint, and sets `details.vision.failed` with no `details.media`.
- A later `browser snapshot` through the same real handler stays text-framed, and the reconstructed multi-turn session carries `total image content blocks: 0`, so nothing base64 rides alongside later `read` / `snapshot` results.
- No-vision path (unchanged): the same handler still reaches `imageResultFromFile` and emits a base64 image block (`image content blocks: 1`). This is the exact tool-result shape the pre-fix catch produced and that `pruneProcessedHistoryImages` preserves for recent turns, so the mechanism is real and the fix is scoped to the configured-vision-failure catch.

Honesty note: the vitest proof mocks only the single vision throw to isolate handler output shapes. The live handler script above uses real Chrome, the real browser control service, the real changed catch path, and the real `describeImageFile` runtime (no mock).

### Handler-side unit and regression tests

Focused tests in `extensions/browser/src/browser-tool.test.ts` drive the real `createBrowserTool().execute()` screenshot path:

- `defangs vision failure fallback text and stays text-only`: vision-failure result is text-only (no `imageResultFromFile`, no image content block, no `details.media`) while preserving the neutralized failure text and share hint.
- `never injects a raw image block when configured vision fails (#106703, #105305)`: configured-vision failure returns zero image content blocks and marks `details.vision.failed`, so the result cannot persist an image across turns.
- No-vision (skipped/unconfigured) path still returns the raw image with sanitization.

target.title: fix(sms): isolate validated webhook quotas per sender
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The SMS webhook's accepted-callback quota was keyed by resolved client address. Twilio shares egress addresses across unrelated senders, so one flooding sender could exhaust the 30/minute callback budget and make valid callbacks from other users fail with HTTP 429.

## Why This Change Was Made

The patch keeps the existing pre-validation failed-request budget keyed by account, route, and client address, but moves the post-validation dispatch quota to account, route, and canonical sender identity.

- Signature-validated callbacks use `resolveTwilioInboundSender(form)`, so equivalent SMS and `RCS:` address forms share one sender bucket.
- A true single-sender overload remains observable as HTTP 429; the handler does not acknowledge and silently discard it.
- Another validated sender behind the same Twilio egress address remains dispatchable.
- With `dangerouslyDisableSignatureValidation`, `From` is unauthenticated, so the stricter callback budget stays keyed to the resolved client address and cannot be bypassed by rotating sender text.

## User Impact

One abusive or bursty sender can no longer cross-throttle unrelated SMS users behind Twilio's shared infrastructure. Existing thresholds and invalid-request behavior remain unchanged, while genuine overload remains fail-closed and visible.

Accepted tradeoff: removing the accidental aggregate egress-IP cap means many distinct signature-validated senders can each use their own 30/minute budget. That is intentional sender isolation; downstream pairing/access policy remains the authorization boundary.

## Evidence

Current contributor head: `16bdfc604bd` on upstream `main` `0483001ef65`.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/sms/src/webhook.test.ts`: focused suite passed, including the new quota-isolation regressions.
- Positive regression: 30 callbacks from sender A are accepted; sender B on the same egress address is still accepted.
- Negative regression: sender A's 31st callback returns 429 even when its address changes from SMS E.164 syntax to equivalent `RCS:+1 (555) 123-4567` syntax and even when the egress IP changes.
- Signature-disabled regression: rotating `From` values does not widen the address-keyed quota.
- Invalid/missing canonical senders share an empty-sender bucket without consuming a valid sender's quota.
- Fixed-window recovery regression: the sender becomes dispatchable after the window expires.
- Direct formatter check and `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` passed.
- The pre-PR plan gate passed for extension, extension-test, and docs lanes with no dependency-sensitive changes.

### Real behavior proof

The focused suite drives the real request-body parser, Twilio HMAC validation, canonical sender resolver, fixed-window limiter, response writer, and durable-ingress seam with realistic HTTP requests. It proves both the intended isolation and the closest bypasses without deploying the Gateway.

No live Twilio callback was sent to this exact branch head, and no Gateway restart or production webhook change was performed. A maintainer-controlled live Twilio smoke remains the strongest optional transport proof.

AI-assisted; reviewed and validated before submission.

## What Problem This Solves

`runQaCli` in `extensions/qa-lab/src/suite-runtime-agent-process.ts` spawns the QA CLI as a detached child and attaches `data` listeners to its `stdout`/`stderr`, but never removed them. After the child closed, the retained listeners kept the stream references alive longer than necessary — a child-process lifecycle cleanup gap.

## Why This Change Was Made

On `close`, detach both stdio `data` listeners (`child.stdout.off("data", onStdout)` / `child.stderr.off("data", onStderr)`). The handlers are named functions so the exact references can be removed. An earlier unconditional `child.unref()` was dropped per review feedback (ineffective for the cleanup goal); the close-time detachment is the retained behavior.

## User Impact

No behavior change for QA suite runs; the parent process no longer retains stdio listeners after the QA CLI child closes.

## Real behavior proof — actual detached QA CLI child run (final head, 2026-07-19)

The exported `runQaCli` was invoked directly on the PR head. It spawned a **real detached subprocess** (`node <repoRoot>/dist/index.js ...`, production spawn path with `detached: true`, piped stdio); a stub CLI stands in for the openclaw entry so the scenario is hermetic — spawn, streams, close handling, and listener cleanup are all the production code path.

target.title: fix(groq): keep default Llama agent turns within TPM limit
target.body:
Closes #104783

AI-assisted with Codex. I reviewed the implementation and the live proof.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running a local agent with `groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile` could receive an immediate HTTP 413 for even a one-word prompt on Groq's 12,000 TPM base tier. The default agent request combined the model's full 32,768-token output capability with the normal prompt and tool schemas, making the request too large before generation began.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Groq plugin leaves the normal first request unchanged. Only a specifically matched Groq HTTP 413 `Request too large` TPM rejection is retried once with tool fields removed and a 1,024-token output limit. The fallback mutation runs after configured payload hooks so they cannot restore the rejected request shape. Explicit max-token overrides skip this recovery policy. Synchronous transport failures retain their normal throw semantics, while asynchronous pre-stream failures retain complete model metadata. The change stays provider- and model-scoped instead of changing shared OpenAI-compatible transport behavior or hard-coding an account's TPM tier as the model capability.

PR #104916 is a competing broader fix that omits implicit output reservations across most OpenAI-compatible transports. These approaches should not both land: this PR intentionally chooses the narrower Groq/model/error-scoped recovery because it has real-provider proof and avoids changing successful requests for other providers.

## User Impact

Default local-agent turns with `groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile` can recover on Groq's base tier instead of failing immediately. Higher-limit organizations retain the existing implicit output budget and normal tool-capable first request, while affected base-tier requests retry with the smaller tool-free payload. Other Groq models and explicitly budgeted requests are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Before, on current `main`, the exact isolated local-agent flow returned HTTP 413: Groq reported `Limit 12000, Requested 61830` for the one-word prompt `你好`.
- The recovery path was live-proven against Groq: the default command first received the narrowly matched HTTP 413, immediately retried without tool fields, and returned HTTP 200 in the same agent attempt. Groq reported 10,071 input tokens and 452 output tokens (10,523 total).
- On the current fallback-only head, a fresh ordinary request reached Groq with its existing implicit budget (`Requested 64910`), proving the first request is not capped at 1,024. Groq then returned an unrelated daily-quota HTTP 429, and OpenClaw correctly made no recovery request. The account reported that the daily quota will reset in about eight hours, so a second successful live recovery could not be run immediately.
- An explicit 128-token budget with the `session_status` tool also returned HTTP 200. Groq reported 8,860 input tokens and 6 output tokens (8,866 total), and the live system-prompt report retained `session_status`.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/groq` — 5 tests passed, including a successful ordinary first request retaining `max_completion_tokens: 32768` and tools, a matching 413 retry canonicalized to only `max_completion_tokens: 1024` when an existing hook tries to restore either or both token aliases plus tools, configured and request-scoped explicit-budget preservation, non-recovery for unrelated 400/401/413-context/429 errors, synchronous throw preservation, and complete asynchronous error metadata.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs extensions/groq/index.test.ts` — clean.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/extensions-test.tsbuildinfo` — clean.
- `node scripts/check-extension-package-tsc-boundary.mjs --help` — all 119 plugin package boundaries compiled, including Groq, plus both canaries.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/groq/index.ts extensions/groq/index.test.ts` — clean.

target.title: fix(channels): stale presence after installing a persisted-auth channel plugin
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who dynamically install (or uninstall, enable/disable, or reload) a plugin that adds a channel with persisted auth state (for example a bundled Matrix/Signal-style channel) would keep seeing the pre-mutation channel presence list. Callers that rely on `config-presence` without passing a fresh discovery result (such as `openclaw doctor` and other non-discovery presence checks) continued to report the stale set of "potentially configured" channels for the lifetime of the process, so a freshly installed channel could be missing from presence output.

## Why This Change Was Made

The module-level `persistedAuthStateChannelIds` cache in `src/channels/config-presence.ts` was populated on first use and never invalidated, so it could not observe registry changes at runtime. The cache is documented as stale after *any* registry mutation or config reload, not only after an installed-package install.

Instead of calling the invalidation from a single install path, this wires `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` into `refreshPluginRegistryAfterConfigMutation` in `src/plugins/registry-refresh.ts` — the single committed boundary that install, uninstall, enable/disable, and config reload all funnel through (via `install-persistence.ts`, `management-service.ts`, `plugins-uninstall-command.ts`, and the update paths). Invalidating there means every registry mutation clears the persisted-auth presence cache, so the next presence scan re-reads bundled plugin metadata. No config shape, protocol, or public presence API changes; the cache remains a process-local single slot.

## User Impact

After dynamically installing, uninstalling, or reloading a plugin that contributes a persisted-auth channel, presence detection (including `openclaw doctor`) now reflects the current channel set without requiring a gateway restart.

## Evidence

- New regression tests in `src/channels/config-presence.test.ts`:
  - Mocked lifecycle tests reproduce the stale-cache behavior across install, uninstall, and multi-cycle mutations, asserting the cache resets and the next read returns the updated channel list.
  - A **real (non-mocked) wiring test** imports the actual shared boundary `refreshPluginRegistryAfterConfigMutation` and asserts it invokes `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` — proving the invalidation is reached through the production registry-mutation path, not just a manually called helper.

### Environment

- Node v24.18.0
- pnpm v11.2.2
- vitest 4.1.10

### Problem Statement
The module-level `persistedAuthStateChannelIds` cache in `src/channels/config-presence.ts` was populated on first use and never invalidated. After an operator installed/uninstalled/reloaded a channel plugin with persisted auth at runtime, presence callers that did not pass a fresh discovery result (e.g. `openclaw doctor`) kept reporting the stale pre-mutation channel list for the process lifetime.

### Fix Summary
Added `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` function and integrated it into `refreshPluginRegistryAfterConfigMutation` — the shared registry-mutation boundary used by install, uninstall, enable/disable, and config reload operations.

target.title: fix(cli): bound dns-cli subprocess probes with timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `brew --prefix` capability probe in `dns-cli.ts` uses `spawnSync` without a timeout. A hung DNS tool shim can block `openclaw dns setup --apply` indefinitely before setup even starts.

## Why This Change Was Made

Prevents indefinite hangs from a misbehaving `brew` probe during DNS setup, without changing the behavior of legitimate long-running setup steps.

## User Impact

No functional change for normal setups. The `brew --prefix` probe is now bounded by a 15s SIGKILL-backed deadline, so a hung (even signal-resistant) probe terminates and the CLI exits with a clear error instead of blocking forever. Install, service restart, and sudo file-write steps keep their previous unbounded wait.

## Evidence

Real environment: macOS (Darwin 24.6.0 arm64), Node v24.18.0, pnpm 11.2.2. Both runs use a real built CLI (`pnpm install && pnpm build`, launched via `node openclaw.mjs`). A controlled hung `brew` shim (`#!/bin/sh` + `exec sleep 3600`) is placed first on `PATH`, so `dns setup --apply` blocks inside the real `brew --prefix` probe in `run()`. The test machine has no Tailscale, so a `NODE_OPTIONS=--import` preload injects a fake `100.64.0.1` interface entry to pass the command's tailnet-IP gate; that gate is unrelated to this change and no production code was modified for the harness. State is isolated via `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/`OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` pointing at a scratch dir.

Exact command:

```sh
node openclaw.mjs dns setup --domain openclaw.internal --apply
```

Before (upstream/main @ 28069db63aa, same harness): the CLI prints the setup plan, then blocks inside the hung probe and never returns; the outer guard kills it after 40s.

```
Tailscale admin (DNS → Nameservers):
- Add nameserver: 100.64.0.1
- Restrict to domain (Split DNS): openclaw.internal
---- result ----
elapsed_seconds=41
exit_code=137
verdict=CLI STILL BLOCKED after 40s guard; killed by harness (unbounded hang)
```

After (this PR @ d41b4ffa10b): the probe's 15s deadline fires, `spawnSync brew ETIMEDOUT` is reported, and the CLI exits with a clear error instead of blocking (~3s CLI startup + 15s timeout = 18s). `ps` afterwards shows no leftover `sleep 3600` process, i.e. SIGKILL reaped the hung probe.

```
Tailscale admin (DNS → Nameservers):
- Add nameserver: 100.64.0.1
- Restrict to domain (Split DNS): openclaw.internal
[openclaw] Could not start the CLI.
[openclaw] Reason: spawnSync brew ETIMEDOUT
[openclaw] Debug: set OPENCLAW_DEBUG=1 to include the stack trace.
[openclaw] Try: openclaw doctor
[openclaw] Help: openclaw --help
---- result ----
elapsed_seconds=18
exit_code=1
leftover hung brew/sleep processes: (none)
verdict=CLI returned on its own after 18s; hung probe SIGKILLed, nothing leaked
```

Regression tests (`pnpm test src/cli/dns-cli.test.ts`):

```
✓ |cli| src/cli/dns-cli.test.ts (2 tests) 62ms
  ✓ bounds the brew prefix probe with a SIGKILL-backed timeout
  ✓ leaves long-running setup subprocesses unbounded
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  2 passed (2)
```

What was not tested: full CoreDNS install end-to-end (requires Homebrew + sudo + a real Tailscale interface on the host); the bounded-probe behavior this PR changes is covered by the controlled hung-subprocess run above, and the unbounded behavior of install/restart/sudo steps is covered by the focused test.

target.title: Bound trajectory pointer file read with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readTrajectoryPointerFile` calls `fs.readFileSync(pointerPath, "utf8")` on session trajectory pointer files with no size limit. A corrupted pointer file can OOM the trajectory cleanup path.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #101472 established the bounded-read pattern for file reads. Trajectory pointer files are small JSON metadata files, but the unbounded `readFileSync` call was a latent vulnerability. Using `readRegularFileSync` with a 1 MB cap (generous for pointer files which are typically <1 KB) prevents OOM from corrupted pointer files.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. Trajectory pointer files are small JSON objects (<1 KB typically); a 1 MB cap is more than sufficient. Corrupted oversized pointer files gracefully return `null` (already handled by the existing try-catch).

## Evidence

- Replaced `fs.readFileSync(pointerPath, "utf8")` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath: pointerPath, maxBytes: TRAJECTORY_POINTER_MAX_BYTES })` at `src/trajectory/cleanup.ts:65-69`
- Added `TRAJECTORY_POINTER_MAX_BYTES = 1 * 1024 * 1024` constant
- Added `readRegularFileSync` import from `../infra/regular-file.js`

target.title: fix(litellm): guard loopback hostname auto-allow with isIP to prevent DNS SSRF bypass
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

LiteLLM image generation automatically permits private-network access for loopback-style endpoints. The previous `127.` prefix check also matched DNS hostnames such as `127.evil.com`, allowing an attacker-controlled public hostname to receive the loopback exemption without the operator's explicit `allowPrivateNetwork` opt-in.

## Why This Change Was Made

The provider now applies the `127/8` exemption only when Node's `net.isIP` confirms that the parsed hostname is an IPv4 literal. This keeps endpoint ownership local to the LiteLLM provider and leaves the shared SSRF policy unchanged. Provider-level regression coverage exercises the canonical image-generation request path, including the explicit opt-in fallback.

The surrounding audit found no second unfixed instance in the same LiteLLM path: Slack and policy helpers already validate literal IPv4 input, the Nostr socket check receives a resolved peer address rather than a URL hostname, and the analogous Codex WebSocket authentication issue is tracked separately in #110692.

## User Impact

Literal `127/8`, `localhost`, IPv6 loopback, and `host.docker.internal` LiteLLM endpoints remain automatic. A DNS hostname beginning with `127.` now needs the existing `models.providers.litellm.request.allowPrivateNetwork` opt-in, as other non-loopback private endpoints already do.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/litellm/image-generation-provider.test.ts` — 1 file passed, 12 tests passed.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs -- extensions/litellm/image-generation-provider.ts extensions/litellm/image-generation-provider.test.ts` — all extension typecheck, test-typecheck, lint, formatting, dependency, boundary, database-first, and import-cycle gates passed on Blacksmith Testbox: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29665469639
- `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode branch --base origin/main --stream-engine-output` — clean; no accepted/actionable findings.
- Node 26.5.0 `net.isIP` probe classified `127.0.0.1` and `127.255.255.255` as IPv4 literals, while classifying `127.evil.com` as not an IP literal.

Fix and tests improved by the OpenClaw maintainer team; original security report and patch by @lsr911.

target.title: Plan grouped Claw agent updates
target.body:
## Summary

- add `openclaw.clawUpdatePlan.v1` for read-only, agent-centric reconciliation of a grouped Claw manifest
- add `openclaw claws update <claw-or-agent> [--from <source>] --dry-run [--json]` behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`
- resolve the normal target from persisted add provenance; keep `--from` as an explicit override and recovery path
- compare effective agent capabilities, workspace files, exact package refs, MCP declarations, and agent-pinned cron declarations
- bind the complete preview to `planIntegrity` for the consented apply slice
- perform no mutation: planning opens existing state read-only, does not create or migrate databases, and closes every owned handle

## Planning contract

- direct agent ids and unambiguous installed package names resolve to one root install record
- older supported databases without Claws tables return structured `claw_not_found`
- missing workspaces and owned artifacts are planned for restoration; unsafe roots, operator drift, ambiguous package identity, and incomplete ownership remain blocked
- blocked actions produce a nonzero CLI result even when no separate diagnostic blocker exists
- independently owned packages and MCP declarations cannot be restored or changed by a Claw
- managed, Claw-introduced resources may be removed only when inspection proves they are unchanged and otherwise unused; referenced or independently owned resources are released
- source MCP config is compared before placeholder resolution so credentials and local substitutions do not create false drift

## Capability and consent contract

- capability changes use secret-safe summaries plus SHA-256 digests; raw MCP configuration and cron payloads never enter the plan model
- effective sandbox values come from OpenClaw's production resolver, including inherited defaults
- widening workspace access, sandbox sharing, tool access, plugin code, MCP surfaces, or scheduled automation requires distinct escalation consent
- reductions and blocked removals do not request escalation consent

## Real behavior proof

Current head: `0eef342ada1275d02142d4702803c09957a9c664`.

An isolated v1 Claw was added with integrity-bound consent, then v2 introduced a remote OAuth MCP URL containing `URL_SECRET_123`, a secret-like tool filter, and cron message `CRON_SECRET_ABC`.

Human preview:

```text
Claw update plan: @proof/safe-preview 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0
Agent: safe-preview
Update actions: 4
Capability changes: 5; escalations requiring distinct consent: 3
  - agent.sandbox.mode: off -> all (change)
  - agent.sandbox.scope: agent -> session (change)
  ! agent.sandbox.workspaceAccess: none -> ro (change)
  ! cronJobs.private-report: unset -> schedule cron; session isolated; payload withheld (add)

```

JSON emitted only paths, classifications, summaries, and digests. It contained none of `secret.example.test`, `URL_SECRET_123`, `PRIVATE_TOOL_SECRET_456`, or `CRON_SECRET_ABC`.

## Verification

- focused update planner and CLI: 46 tests passed
- real Claw lifecycle E2E: 8 tests passed
- broader Claw unit coverage: 95 tests passed during the restack
- Oxfmt, focused Oxlint, repository guardrails, import-cycle checks, and `git diff --check` passed

- `codex review --base ec41651ee29aa40573420ef00b038c56d155a797`: accepted findings fixed; one source-migration suggestion rejected because valid Claw packages constrain `source` to the literal `"clawhub"`

- This PR: authoritative read-only update planning and consent boundary
- Next: #102982 executes only a freshly rebuilt, unblocked, consent-matched plan

target.title: feat(config): add compaction.thinkingLevel to override thinking level during compaction
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Embedded compaction inherited the active turn's thinking level, so operators could not tune summary cost and quality independently from ordinary turns.

## Why This Change Was Made

The maintainer rewrite adds the optional `agents.defaults.compaction.thinkingLevel` setting across the exported config type, schema, help metadata, generated plugin SDK baseline, and docs. All nine supported thinking levels are accepted.

For embedded compaction, the configured override wins over the inherited turn level, then is revalidated and clamped for every concrete provider, model, and runtime candidate, including fallbacks. When unset, existing inherited behavior is preserved.

Native Codex app-server compaction warns and ignores this setting because the upstream compact operation currently exposes only a thread identifier and has no per-operation reasoning parameter.

## User Impact

Operators can use a lower or higher reasoning level for embedded compaction without changing ordinary turns, while unsupported levels are handled by the same capability-aware resolver as normal model selection.

## Release Note

Agent defaults now support `compaction.thinkingLevel` for embedded compaction summaries, with concrete-model validation and an explicit warning for native Codex compaction. Thanks @mpz4life.

target.title: fix(sessions): read pinned session-extension registry in upstream monitor
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The session upstream monitor resolved catalog providers from the **mutable** plugin registry state (`getPluginRegistryState()?.activeRegistry`). When a standalone plugin load swaps that registry, the monitor can silently lose sight of the providers backing adopted-session upstream watches — upstream activity for watched sessions stops being observed until the next registry churn happens to restore them.

## Why This Change Was Made

Switch the monitor's provider source to the **pinned** session-extension registry (`getActivePluginSessionExtensionRegistry`), the same source the session-catalog path already trusts. The pinned registry survives mutable-registry swaps, so watched upstream links keep resolving to their catalog providers across plugin reloads.

## User Impact

Adopted-session upstream monitoring keeps working across plugin registry churn instead of intermittently missing upstream activity. No configuration or API change.

## Real behavior proof — multi-plugin registry churn (final head `c8be3d57`, 2026-07-19)

Runtime trace executing the **real** plugin runtime (`src/plugins/runtime.ts`), state database (SQLite in a temp state dir), and the real monitor tick (`src/sessions/session-upstream-monitor.ts`) — no mocks of the monitor or registry plumbing. The pinned registry carries **two** providers; the mutable registry is churned twice, the second time with a rogue provider that must never be consulted.

```bash
./node_modules/.bin/tsx registry-churn-proof.mts
```

```text
date: Sun Jul 19 2026 07:38:22 GMT+0800 (中国标准时间)
node: v24.18.0
modules: src/plugins/runtime.ts + src/sessions/session-upstream-monitor.ts @ PR head
state dir: /var/folders/…/openclaw-pinned-registry-proof-Sex0IS
[setup] mutable active registry swapped in (empty — simulates plugin reload churn)
[setup] pinned session-extension registry carries providers: "claude", "codex"
[setup] watched catalogs: claude, codex
[tick 1] before churn:
  -> provider "claude" checkUpstreamActivity called with 1 probe(s)
  -> provider "codex" checkUpstreamActivity called with 1 probe(s)
[churn] mutable active registry replaced; now carries only "rogue"
[tick 2] after churn:
  -> provider "claude" checkUpstreamActivity called with 1 probe(s)
  -> provider "codex" checkUpstreamActivity called with 1 probe(s)
[result] provider calls: ["claude","codex","claude","codex"]
[result] PASS: monitor kept using the pinned providers across churn; rogue never called
```

Both pinned providers are consulted on every tick; the mutable registry's contents (empty first, then a rogue provider) never influence the monitor.

## Regression tests (final head)

```bash
pnpm vitest run src/sessions/session-upstream-monitor-pinned-registry.test.ts
```

```text
Tests  1 passed (1)
```

## What was not tested

A full multi-plugin Gateway process trace (with real plugin hosts and model providers) was not produced — the trace above runs the exact monitor and registry code paths against a real state database, which is where the provider-source selection lives. No endpoints, credentials, or room IDs involved, so nothing required redaction.

## Rebase status

Branch rebased onto latest `origin/main` at head `c8be3d57`; required checks re-run on the exact head.

target.title: fix(e2e): bound non-root installer fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The non-root install-sh Docker smoke runner fetches the official installer and pipes it straight into bash. Current `origin/main` bounds that pipe with `--connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300`, but it still streams the payload directly into the shell and uses a much looser budget than the sibling e2e runner:

```sh
# scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh (current origin/main)
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300 -- "$INSTALL_URL" | bash
```

This PR brings the non-root runner to the same **download-then-execute** contract as the sibling e2e runner merged in #108810 (`scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh`): download the installer to a temp file with explicit connect/total timeouts, verify curl completed, then execute it, then clean up.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Fail fast on stall:** `--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120` matches the values already merged for the sibling installer/download fixes in this area (#108810, #108911). A stalled fetch fails the step in under 2 minutes instead of tying up the runner for 5.
- **No partial-stream execution:** with the temp-file form, bash only ever runs a fully downloaded installer; curl's exit status gates execution (`set -euo pipefail`).
- **Consistency:** both Docker install-sh lanes now share the same fetch contract.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change to the installer itself. This only affects the non-root install-sh Docker CI lane: a stalled installer download fails fast with a clear curl error instead of streaming into a long-hanging pipe. Identical install semantics on success.

## Evidence

After (this PR, `scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh`):

```sh
echo "==> Run installer (non-root user)"
# Download the installer to a temp file first so a stalled connection or hung
# response body cannot wedge the container run forever. Piping curl straight to
# bash inherits curl's default of no total timeout.
installer="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$installer"' EXIT
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer" "$INSTALL_URL"
bash "$installer"
```

Regression tests (final head `15ad709b`, rebased onto latest main):

```bash
pnpm vitest run test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts
```

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  77 passed (77)
```

Coverage includes a controlled stalled-transfer probe: the bounded fetch aborts on stall (the exact failure mode this change defends against), and the temp installer file is cleaned up via the EXIT trap. The runner-assertion test now checks the bounded temp-file form (`--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer"` + `bash "$installer"`).

## What was not tested

A live successful non-root **Docker** smoke run against the real installer endpoint: this contributor environment has no container runtime, so no Docker transcript is attached. Behavior on the success path is unchanged apart from the fetch budget (curl flags and execution order are asserted by the suite above); the stall path is proven hermetically.

## CI note

The previous head failed `checks-node-compact-small-1` because the branch's own runner assertion still expected the old piped form (`curl ... | bash`) that this PR replaces. The assertion is aligned with the temp-file fetch on the current head, and the branch is rebased onto latest main.

target.title: Plan grouped Claw agent updates
target.body:
## Summary

- add `openclaw.clawUpdatePlan.v1` for read-only, agent-centric reconciliation of a grouped Claw manifest
- add `openclaw claws update <claw-or-agent> [--from <source>] --dry-run [--json]` behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`
- resolve the normal target from persisted add provenance; keep `--from` as an explicit override and recovery path
- compare effective agent capabilities, workspace files, exact package refs, MCP declarations, and agent-pinned cron declarations
- bind the complete preview to `planIntegrity` for the consented apply slice
- perform no mutation: planning opens existing state read-only, does not create or migrate databases, and closes every owned handle

## Planning contract

- direct agent ids and unambiguous installed package names resolve to one root install record
- older supported databases without Claws tables return structured `claw_not_found`
- missing workspaces and owned artifacts are planned for restoration; unsafe roots, operator drift, ambiguous package identity, and incomplete ownership remain blocked
- blocked actions produce a nonzero CLI result even when no separate diagnostic blocker exists
- independently owned packages and MCP declarations cannot be restored or changed by a Claw
- managed, Claw-introduced resources may be removed only when inspection proves they are unchanged and otherwise unused; referenced or independently owned resources are released
- source MCP config is compared before placeholder resolution so credentials and local substitutions do not create false drift

## Capability and consent contract

- capability changes use secret-safe summaries plus SHA-256 digests; raw MCP configuration and cron payloads never enter the plan model
- effective sandbox values come from OpenClaw's production resolver, including inherited defaults
- widening workspace access, sandbox sharing, tool access, plugin code, MCP surfaces, or scheduled automation requires distinct escalation consent
- reductions and blocked removals do not request escalation consent

## Real behavior proof

Current head: `0eef342ada1275d02142d4702803c09957a9c664`.

An isolated v1 Claw was added with integrity-bound consent, then v2 introduced a remote OAuth MCP URL containing `URL_SECRET_123`, a secret-like tool filter, and cron message `CRON_SECRET_ABC`.

Human preview:

```text
Claw update plan: @proof/safe-preview 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0
Agent: safe-preview
Update actions: 4
Capability changes: 5; escalations requiring distinct consent: 3
  - agent.sandbox.mode: off -> all (change)
  - agent.sandbox.scope: agent -> session (change)
  ! agent.sandbox.workspaceAccess: none -> ro (change)
  ! cronJobs.private-report: unset -> schedule cron; session isolated; payload withheld (add)
  ! mcpServers.private-search: unset -> remote server; auth configured; tool filter configured (add)
```

JSON emitted only paths, classifications, summaries, and digests. It contained none of `secret.example.test`, `URL_SECRET_123`, `PRIVATE_TOOL_SECRET_456`, or `CRON_SECRET_ABC`.

## Verification

- focused update planner and CLI: 46 tests passed
- real Claw lifecycle E2E: 8 tests passed
- broader Claw unit coverage: 95 tests passed during the restack
- Oxfmt, focused Oxlint, repository guardrails, import-cycle checks, and `git diff --check` passed
- direct core tsgo reached only the existing shared `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` dependency errors; changed files reported no type errors
- `codex review --base ec41651ee29aa40573420ef00b038c56d155a797`: accepted findings fixed; one source-migration suggestion rejected because valid Claw packages constrain `source` to the literal `"clawhub"`

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102427 read-only diagnostics
- This PR: authoritative read-only update planning and consent boundary
- Next: #102982 executes only a freshly rebuilt, unblocked, consent-matched plan

target.title: fix(extensions): bound extension source read with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `extensionSourceNeedsJitiAliasResolution` function reads entire extension source files into memory with no size bound. Extension source files can be large (compiled bundles, bundled dependencies), risking OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

The function used raw `fs.readFileSync(extensionPath, "utf8")` with no size pre-check. The fix adds a `statSync` pre-check that:

1. Verifies the path is a regular file
2. Rejects files exceeding 10 MiB by returning `true` (assumes jiti alias resolution is needed)
3. Only then reads content with `readFileSync` and scans for import patterns

## User Impact

- Prevents OOM crashes when scanning large extension source files
- Oversized extensions are still loaded (via jiti) — no functionality lost

target.title: fix(boot-echo): keep echo guard chunking UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `boot-echo-guard.ts` uses `String.prototype.slice()` to extract fixed-length chunks from the normalized boot prompt and outbound response text for echo comparison. Since JavaScript's `slice()` operates on UTF-16 code units, a chunk boundary can land in the middle of a surrogate pair (e.g., emoji like 🎈 U+1F388, some CJK characters). This produces a substring with a dangling lone surrogate, which never matches an entry in the chunk `Set<string>` built from the other side — causing a false negative where boot context echoes go undetected.

**Solution**: Replace `String.prototype.slice(i, i + minLen)` with `sliceUtf16SafeMinLen(input, i, minLen)` which delegates to `sliceUtf16Safe()` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`. The safe-slicing function adjusts the start offset forward when it lands on a low surrogate and the end offset backward when it lands after a high surrogate, ensuring every chunk and every probe is a valid UTF-16 substring.

**What changed**: Two call sites in `getBootPromptChunks()` (line 49) and `containsSubstantialBootEcho()` (line 100) — each `haystack.slice(i, i + minLen)` or `normalizedBootPrompt.slice(i, i + minLen)` becomes `sliceUtf16SafeMinLen(input, i, minLen)`. The helper also enforces `minLen` via `start + minLen` rather than dynamic `end`, matching the existing chunk-size contract. A new `sliceUtf16SafeMinLen` wrapper function ensures at least `minLen` characters are returned.

**What not changed**: No behavioral change for ASCII-only or BMP text; no external API surface modified; no new dependencies.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: UTF-16 surrogate-boundary unsafe chunking in boot-echo-guard's echo detection sliding-window algorithm.

**Real environment tested**: Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux 6.17.0-40-generic), Node.js v25.9.0, OpenClaw source with the fix applied.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
cd /home/lizeyu/workspace/openclaw/.worktree/pr-110641
node --import tsx docs/.local/issue-110641/verify.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
=== 1. sliceUtf16Safe at surrogate boundaries ===
Input: "Hello🎈World🔥End" (length=17 UTF-16 code units)

  include full 🎈 at boundary:
    .slice(0, 6)         → "Hello\ud83c" (len=6, BROKEN)
    sliceUtf16Safe(0, 6) → "Hello" (len=5, SAFE)

  low surrogate only (should be empty or 1 char):
    .slice(6, 7)         → "\udf88" (len=1, BROKEN)
    sliceUtf16Safe(6, 7) → "" (len=0, SAFE)

=== 2. Echo guard with surrogate-heavy boot prompt ===
Output: ""
Echo detected: YES ✅  (echo containing 30 balloon emoji correctly stripped)

=== 3. Normal (non-surrogate) echo detection unchanged ===
Echo detected: YES ✅  (ASCII-only echo still works)

=== 4. Non-echo text with surrogates is not stripped ===
Kept as-is: YES ✅  (no false positive on "I really like 🎈 balloons!")
```

**Observed result after the fix**: `sliceUtf16Safe` avoids slicing through surrogate pairs. When the start offset lands on a low surrogate, it advances by 1 to skip to the next complete character. When the end offset lands right after a high surrogate, it retreats by 1. The result is that every chunk key inserted into the echo-comparison `Set` and every probe substring is a well-formed UTF-16 sequence. The sliding-window algorithm thus produces matching entries for both the boot prompt and the outbound response even when surrogate-heavy content appears near chunk boundaries.

**What was not tested**: Real end-to-end LLM responses containing CJK text with surrogate pairs >U+FFFF, mixed-directionality scripts, or 4+ byte emoji ZWJ sequences (e.g., family emoji composed of multiple surrogate pairs). The `sliceUtf16Safe` unit test suite covers the surrogate-boundary edge cases for those inputs; the integration test here confirms the boot-echo-guard pipeline with emoji-heavy content.

## Tests and validation

- Unit tests: `src/gateway/boot-echo-guard.test.ts` — 6 tests, all pass (18 tests in file group)
- Unit tests: `packages/normalization-core/src/utf16-slice.test.ts` — surrogate-boundary slicing coverage
- Manual verification: dedicated verify.ts script exercises surrogate-boundary slicing, surrogate-heavy echo detection, non-surrogate echo detection, and false-positive-free behavior with surrogate content
- CI: 10 green checks on the PR

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(grep): bound file reads with size cap in default grep operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The default `readFile` operation in the grep tool reads files with no size bound. When grep matches lines in a large file (e.g., a multi-GB log file), `getFileLines` loads the entire file into memory to render context, risking OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `defaultGrepOperations.readFile` function at line 68 used raw `fs.readFileSync(p, "utf-8")` with no size pre-check. The fix adds a `statSync` pre-check that:

1. Verifies the path is a regular file (not a directory or device)
2. Rejects files exceeding 50 MiB with a clear error
3. Only then reads content with `readFileSync`

The error is caught by `getFileLines` (line 239), which returns empty lines on error — the same graceful degradation as other read failures.

## User Impact

- Prevents OOM crashes when grep matches lines in oversized files
- Context lines for oversized files show as unreadable (same behavior as permission errors)
- No change for normal files under 50 MiB

## Evidence

**`pnpm test src/agents/sessions/tools/grep.stream-errors.test.ts`** — all 8 existing tests pass:
```

```

target.title: fix(sessions): bound AGENTS.md and prompt-input file reads with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Two file read paths in the session resource loader read files without any size bound, risking OOM from large or corrupted files:

1. **`resolvePromptInput`** — reads user-supplied `--system-prompt` and `--append-system-prompt` files with unbounded `readFileSync`. A user could accidentally (or maliciously) point this at a multi-GB file, exhausting memory.

2. **`loadContextFileFromDir`** — reads `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` project context files with unbounded `readFileSync`. These files are user-authored and can be arbitrarily large.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both paths use raw `fs.readFileSync` with no limit on file size. The fix adds a `readTextFileSafely` helper that:

1. `statSync` the file first to check it is a regular file
2. Rejects files exceeding the byte cap with a clear warning
3. Only then reads content with `readFileSync`

Caps:
- **AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md context files**: 1 MiB — these are project metadata files, not meant to be large
- **User-supplied prompt input files**: 10 MiB — these can include larger instructions but still capped

## User Impact

- Prevents OOM crashes from oversized input files during session startup
- Preserves warning logs for non-regular-file paths (directories, devices)
- Gracefully skips oversized files instead of crashing the process

## Evidence

**`pnpm test src/agents/sessions/resource-loader.test.ts`** — all 5 tests pass:

- "does not use unreadable prompt file paths as prompt content" — existing test preserved
- "rejects oversized system prompt files" — 11 MiB file rejected with warning
- "accepts system prompt files within the byte limit" — normal file loads correctly
- "skips oversized AGENTS.md files during context file loading" — 2 MiB AGENTS.md skipped
- "loads AGENTS.md files within the byte limit" — normal AGENTS.md loads correctly

```

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
```

## Summary

Fixes #109992

**What changed**: Added `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in the `postCrablineInbound()` error path. When a Crabline inbound injection returns a non-ok HTTP status, the response body ReadableStream is now explicitly cancelled before throwing the error, preventing an unread stream resource leak.

**What NOT changed**: No change to the happy path — successful responses still pass through to the complete handler as before. No change to the Crabline injection logic, request construction, or error message format. No new dependencies added.

**merge-risk**: Minimal — the pattern `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` is a standard no-op on success and a no-throw guard on failure. It affects only the single error path in `crabline-transport.ts`. Zero risk of regression on the ok path.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When a Crabline inbound injection HTTP request returns a non-ok response (e.g., 502, 400), the response body stream is left unread, causing a potential resource leak (unconsumed ReadableStream). Node.js will emit a warning for unconsumed response bodies in future versions.

**Root Cause**: `postCrablineInbound()` throws immediately in the `if (!response.ok)` branch without cancelling the unread response body, leaving the stream open for garbage collection to clean up — which is non-deterministic and can retain buffers until GC runs.

**Solution**: Add `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in the error path to eagerly release the stream. The `cancel()` method (Fetch API standard) releases the stream's resources. The `?.` optional chaining guards against a null body (e.g., 204 No Content responses or server errors that omit a body). The `.catch()` ensures that a double-cancel or rejection from the stream implementation does not propagate.

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: When a Crabline inbound injection receives a non-ok HTTP response (e.g., 502, 400), the response body stream is now explicitly cancelled before the error is thrown, eliminating a resource leak from an unconsumed ReadableStream.

## Summary

`loadRuntimeParityMockToolCalls` fetches the `debug/requests` endpoint from a configured QA Lab runtime parity server. When the endpoint returns a non-ok HTTP status (503, 400, 500), the function returns null early without consuming the response body stream, leaving an unread stream resource dangling that may hold the connection open.

The fix adds `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the early return on `!response.ok`. This cancels the unread body stream, matching the resource cleanup that `response.json()` implicitly performs on the ok path.

**What changed**: One line added in `loadRuntimeParityMockToolCalls` at `runtime-parity.ts:1055`. No changes to the ok path, parity logic, error handling flow, or any other functionality.

**What NOT changed**: No changes to the ok response path, parity logic, error handling flow, or any other functionality. No new dependencies or configuration options added.

Fixes #109991

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: `loadRuntimeParityMockToolCalls` returns null early on non-ok HTTP responses without cancelling the unread response body stream, potentially leaking resources and holding connections open.

**Root Cause**: At `runtime-parity.ts:1055`, the `!response.ok` early-return path calls `return null` without first cancelling the response body stream via `response.body?.cancel()`. The ok path implicitly drains the body via `response.json()`, but the non-ok path has no such cleanup.

**Solution**: Add `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before returning null on non-ok responses. This mirrors the resource cleanup that `response.json()` implicitly performs on the ok path. The `.catch(() => undefined)` guard ensures safety even if the body stream is already in an inconsistent state.

target.body:
## Summary

**What changed**: Two fixes in this PR.

1. **qa-lab: cancel unread response body on HTTP error** — Add `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing on non-2xx responses in `getJson`/`getJsonNoStore` so the connection is released back to the pool.
2. **vertex-adc: guard JSON.parse against malformed credential files** — Wrap `JSON.parse` in try-catch with a descriptive error message including the file path instead of a raw `SyntaxError`.

**What NOT changed**: `postJson` is intentionally left unchanged — it reads the error response body to extract error payloads, so body cancel would interfere. The Vertex ADC change only affects the error message format; behavior (returning `undefined` on invalid credentials) is preserved.

Fixes #109985

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**:
- QA Lab HTTP: When `getJson`/`getJsonNoStore` receive a non-2xx HTTP status, they throw without consuming the response body. The underlying connection stays open (not returned to the pool), which can exhaust the connection pool under error storms.
- Vertex ADC: A malformed credential file at `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` causes a raw `SyntaxError` from `JSON.parse`, giving users no indication of which file is broken.

**Root Cause**:
- QA Lab HTTP: `getJson`/`getJsonNoStore` call `response.json()` only on success. On error they throw immediately without consuming or cancelling `response.body`. The body reader holds a reference to the underlying TCP socket, preventing connection reuse.
- Vertex ADC: `readGoogleAdcCredentials` calls `JSON.parse(text)` without a try-catch, so any invalid JSON raises an unhelpful `SyntaxError` with no path context.

**Solution**:
- QA Lab HTTP: Insert `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in both `getJson` and `getJsonNoStore`. Optional chaining handles null body; `.catch()` suppresses cancellation rejections.
- Vertex ADC: Wrap `JSON.parse(text)` in try-catch that throws `new Error(\`Google Vertex ADC credentials must be valid JSON: ${adcPath}\`)`.

## Evidence

### Fix 1: QA Lab HTTP body cancel

**Real environment tested**:
Node.js 22, vitest 4.1.10, Linux 6.17.0-40-generic

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
npx vitest run extensions/qa-lab/web/src/http.evidence.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

```
 ✓ |extension-qa| http.evidence.test.ts > QA Lab HTTP body cancel on HTTP error > getJson 500: body cancelled 1ms

 ✓ |extension-qa| http.evidence.test.ts > QA Lab HTTP body cancel on HTTP error > Cancel rejection: suppressed 1ms
```

**Observed result after the fix**:
All non-2xx paths call `response.body?.cancel()` before throwing, verified across status codes 400, 403, 429, 500, 503. Null body and cancellation rejection edge cases are also handled.

**What was not tested**:
`postJson` was not modified — it reads the error response body via `response.json()` to extract an error payload, so body cancel would interfere.

### Fix 2: Vertex ADC JSON.parse guard

**Real environment tested**:
Node.js 22, vitest 4.1.10, Linux 6.17.0-40-generic

```bash
npx vitest run extensions/google/vertex-adc.evidence.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

Both paths are covered: (a) via the integration test above, and (b) via the error-recovery path — if credentials are invalid, the function throws, which is caught upstream and falls through to `google-auth-library`.

target.title: fix(imessage): prevent duplicate messages after delayed sends
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an iMessage send could complete through `imsg`'s AppleScript fallback after a private-bridge stall, while OpenClaw reported a timeout to the calling agent. The agent then retried the apparently failed send, producing duplicate messages.

## Why This Change Was Made

The dedicated send timeout is increased from 150 seconds to 180 seconds. This lets the outer RPC outlive `imsg`'s 150-second bridge deadline plus its fallback verification window, while leaving the 10-second probe timeout unchanged.

This is intentionally a boundary fix rather than a second delivery-verification implementation in OpenClaw. In the observed incident, the delivered rows stored their text in `attributedBody`, so OpenClaw's plain `message.text` recovery path could not reliably identify them. `imsg` already owns that verification.

## User Impact

Users should receive one message instead of duplicates when the private iMessage bridge stalls but the fallback send succeeds.

## Evidence

### Redacted live failure timeline before the fix

One cron session issued three sends of the same text to the same chat:

```text
09:00:33  send request 1 started
09:03:14  OpenClaw reported imsg rpc timeout (send); outgoing row 7080 persisted
09:03:19  calling agent retried
09:05:57  OpenClaw reported imsg rpc timeout (send); outgoing row 7081 persisted
09:06:19  calling agent used direct imsg send; outgoing row 7082 persisted
```

Recipient and message text are omitted. The matching timeout and persistence timestamps show that the first two sends completed at the point the 150-second outer timer rejected them.

### Dependency and caller contract

- `imsg` assigns send actions a [150-second bridge deadline](https://github.com/openclaw/imsg/blob/ca91c41b47e0bbe75b6ac599b583531ff9fa67d2/Sources/IMsgCore/IMsgBridgeProtocol.swift#L28-L39), which its [bridge client enforces](https://github.com/openclaw/imsg/blob/ca91c41b47e0bbe75b6ac599b583531ff9fa67d2/Sources/IMsgCore/IMsgBridgeClient.swift#L97-L121).
- Auto transport [falls through to AppleScript after a bridge error and then verifies the persisted send](https://github.com/openclaw/imsg/blob/ca91c41b47e0bbe75b6ac599b583531ff9fa67d2/Sources/imsg/RPCServer%2BHandlers.swift#L271-L320).
- The persisted-message verifier [polls for up to 8 seconds](https://github.com/openclaw/imsg/blob/ca91c41b47e0bbe75b6ac599b583531ff9fa67d2/Sources/imsg/SentMessageVerifier.swift#L13-L26).
- OpenClaw selects the dedicated default in [`sendMessageIMessage`](https://github.com/omarshahine/openclaw/blob/fce7399810c/extensions/imessage/src/send.ts#L720-L725) and [passes it to the single RPC request](https://github.com/omarshahine/openclaw/blob/fce7399810c/extensions/imessage/src/send.ts#L871-L885). OpenClaw does not retry this request internally; the calling agent retried after receiving the ambiguous timeout.

### Deterministic delayed-boundary proof

The focused regression test models `imsg` returning successfully at 158 seconds, after the old outer deadline but within the new one. It asserts that the send resolves with the fallback message GUID and that OpenClaw makes exactly one RPC request.

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       52 passed (52)
```

Command: `pnpm exec vitest run extensions/imessage/src/send.test.ts`

### Live patched-build proof

The branch was rebased onto current `main`, built, and run through Lobster's exclusive iMessage dev-gateway proof workflow. A temporary copy of the morning context-question cron was triggered once with an explicit private destination:

```text
status:          ok
duration:        5207 ms
deliveryStatus:  delivered
database rows:   1
row:             7086 at 10:58:38 local time
```

The recipient, message text, and GUID are omitted. The unique output persisted as exactly one outgoing row. This live run completed through the normal fast bridge path; the 158-second fallback boundary is covered deterministically above because forcing a real bridge stall would require restarting Messages with a stale readiness marker and would introduce an avoidable delivery race.

After proof, the temporary dev cron was removed, the dev gateway stopped, and production was restored healthy on port 18789 with exactly one `imsg rpc` process.

Additional validation:

- Full branch build passed on current `main`.
- `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check` pass.
- Final Codex branch autoreview: no findings; patch rated correct with 0.94 confidence.

AI-assisted: diagnosis, implementation, test updates, and independent review were performed with Codex under maintainer supervision.

target.title: fix(openai-http): keep SSE argument chunking UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## Summary

Replace `String.prototype.slice()` with `sliceUtf16Safe()` in `splitArgumentsForStreaming` to prevent SSE argument chunks from splitting UTF-16 surrogate pairs. The old code could produce invalid JSON when multi-byte characters (e.g., CJK, emoji) straddled the 256-char chunk boundary, causing downstream parse failures on the client.

Fixes #110642

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: SSE streaming chunks of tool_call arguments can contain truncated/invalid UTF-16 when the 256-char boundary falls inside a surrogate pair, causing the client to receive malformed JSON.

**Root Cause**: `splitArgumentsForStreaming()` in `src/gateway/openai-http.ts` uses `String.prototype.slice()` which operates on UTF-16 code units without awareness of surrogate pairs. When a multi-byte character spans positions 255-256, the slice produces a broken chunk.

**Solution**: Import and use `sliceUtf16Safe()` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, which ensures surrogate pairs are never split. The loop increment is changed from a fixed `+= chunkSize` to `+= chunk.length` (with `|| 1` fallback) because the safe slice may return 256 or 257 characters.

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: SSE chunking of tool_call arguments to not split UTF-16 surrogate pairs

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-40-generic / vitest 4.1.10 / OpenClaw worktree

`loadSessionStoreForSnapshotScan` had a broad catch that silently swallowed all errors from corrupt JSON or unreadable snapshot stores, returning `{}`. This prevented the caller from diagnosing the failure — a corrupt store was indistinguishable from an empty one.

target.title: fix(ssh-verify): preserve active cooldown entries during prune
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: The cooldown prune function's size-bound enforcement loop (`while` loop in `pruneCooldowns`) evicts the oldest entry without checking whether it is still active (unexpired). This means a cooldown entry that is still in effect — where `expiry > nowMs` — could be evicted just because the cache is over `MAX_COOLDOWN_ENTRIES`, causing the system to re-probe a recently failed host before its cooldown period has elapsed.

**Root Cause**: The `while` loop that enforces the hard size bound (`MAX_COOLDOWN_ENTRIES = 512`) on `cooldownExpiryByKey` unconditionally deletes the oldest entry when the map exceeds the limit. Unlike the `for` loop above it (which only removes expired entries), the `while` loop has no guard to distinguish expired entries (safe to evict) from active ones (must be preserved).

**Solution**: Before evicting the oldest entry in the size-bound enforcement loop, read its expiry and check whether it is still active (`expiry > nowMs`). If it is, break out of the loop — the cache is over-full only with active entries, which should not be evicted. The `for` loop above already handles cleanup of expired entries.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: CI test suite (unit tests for `node-pairing-ssh-verify` module)

```
npx vitest run src/gateway/node-pairing-ssh-verify.test.ts
```

target.title: fix(ui): bound Nostr profile write/read requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` helpers in `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts` issue `fetch` requests to the gateway/relay Nostr profile endpoint **without any timeout or abort signal**. A stalled or unreachable endpoint hangs the channels page indefinitely while it awaits the response.

This mirrors the same class of unbounded-network-operation fixes (e.g. `fix(ci)`, `fix(docker)`, `fix(doctor)` "bound X" PRs): an unterminated request with no `AbortSignal` can block the UI forever.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add an `AbortController` + `setTimeout` watchdog (`NOSTR_PROFILE_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000`) to both fetches, following the existing Control UI convention used by `browser-client.ts`, `custom-theme.ts`, and `agent-select.ts`. The timeout is cleared in `finally` so no timer leaks.

## User Impact

The channels Nostr profile publish/import actions now fail fast instead of hanging when the relay is slow or down.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** Nostr profile publish/import (`putNostrProfile`, `importNostrProfile`) hang the channels page forever when the gateway/relay endpoint never responds, because the fetch has no abort signal.

**Real environment tested:** macOS 15, Node v24.18.0, vitest 4.1.10, local HTTP server (`node:http`) bound to 127.0.0.1:0. **Real wall-clock time** is used (not fake timers) to prove actual timeout behavior.

**Exact commands run:**
```bash
# Fake-timer regression tests (fast CI feedback)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts

# Real-timeout behavior proof (actual wall-clock validation)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts --reporter=verbose

# Type-suppression inventory (repo-wide guard that previously failed on this branch)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/type-suppression-inventory.test.ts
```

**Terminal output showing real timeout behavior:**
```
$ node -v
v24.18.0

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 RUN  v4.1.10 /Users/maomaoplanet/workspace/openclaw-worktrees/pr-110009

stdout | ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts > Nostr profile operations with real timeouts > aborts a stalled putNostrProfile after the real 15s bound instead of hanging
[REAL TIMEOUT] putNostrProfile aborted after 15016ms
[REAL TIMEOUT] Error type: AbortError
[REAL TIMEOUT] Error message: This operation was aborted

 ✓ |ui| ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts > Nostr profile operations with real timeouts > aborts a stalled putNostrProfile after the real 15s bound instead of hanging 15013ms
stdout | ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts > Nostr profile operations with real timeouts > aborts a stalled importNostrProfile after the real 15s bound instead of hanging
[REAL TIMEOUT] importNostrProfile aborted after 15006ms
[REAL TIMEOUT] Error type: AbortError
[REAL TIMEOUT] Error message: This operation was aborted

stdout | ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts > Nostr profile operations with real timeouts > resolves a normal putNostrProfile round trip quickly
[NORMAL] putNostrProfile completed in 15ms

stdout | ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts > Nostr profile operations with real timeouts > resolves a normal importNostrProfile round trip quickly
[NORMAL] importNostrProfile completed in 4ms

 ✓ |ui| ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts > Nostr profile operations with real timeouts > aborts a stalled importNostrProfile after the real 15s bound instead of hanging 15006ms
 ✓ |ui| ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts > Nostr profile operations with real timeouts > resolves a normal putNostrProfile round trip quickly 17ms
 ✓ |ui| ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.real-timeout.test.ts > Nostr profile operations with real timeouts > resolves a normal importNostrProfile round trip quickly 5ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
   Start at  06:24:29
   Duration  30.36s (transform 19ms, setup 11ms, import 12ms, tests 30.04s, environment 240ms)
```

**Terminal output showing regression suite (fake timers) and type-suppression guard:**
```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts
 ✓ |ui| ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts (6 tests) 25ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
   Duration  621ms (transform 43ms, setup 31ms, import 7ms, tests 25ms, environment 486ms)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/type-suppression-inventory.test.ts
 ✓ keeps unchecked any casts at zero and negative type assertions explicit  2545ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Duration  2.84s (transform 98ms, setup 29ms, import 177ms, tests 2.55s, environment 0ms)
```

**Observed result after fix:**
- Stalled `putNostrProfile` aborts after exactly **15,016ms** (within the 15s bound) and raises `AbortError`
- Stalled `importNostrProfile` aborts after exactly **15,006ms** (within the 15s bound) and raises `AbortError`
- Normal `putNostrProfile` requests complete in **15ms** (fast, no timeout)
- Normal `importNostrProfile` requests complete in **4ms** (fast, no timeout)
- All timeout tests pass with real wall-clock time, proving the abort mechanism works correctly
- Error type is correctly `AbortError` with message "This operation was aborted"

**What was tested:**
- Real wall-clock timeout behavior (not fake timers) against a deliberately stalled local HTTP server
- Normal operation round trips complete in milliseconds
- AbortError is correctly raised and can be caught/handled by UI code
- Timeout mechanism works for both publish and import operations
- Both quick-regression tests (fake timers) and real-behavior tests (real timers) pass
- The real-timeout suite saves the original `globalThis.fetch` before installing its relative-URL bridge and restores it in `afterEach`, so no bridge leaks into later tests; both Nostr suites were rerun after this teardown repair (results above)
- The repo-wide type-suppression inventory passes (`as-any` count stays at 0); the fetch bridge assigns `globalThis.fetch` through the standard typed signature
- No persistent data-model change: the diff only touches the two Nostr profile helpers and their test files; nothing is serialized, stored, or migrated

**Key difference from prior evidence:** This uses actual wall-clock time to demonstrate the timeout mechanism, providing real runtime behavior proof that the UI will fail fast after 15 seconds instead of hanging indefinitely. The tests prove the error is recoverable (AbortError can be caught and handled).
